# SK1053 — Use a discard

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A named local that exists only to receive a value nobody reads — a return value kept for the call's effect, or an `out var` the caller does not want.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | 7.0 |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

A name is a claim that something will be referred to again. When nothing refers to it, the name is a small lie the reader has to check: they look for the second use, do not find it, and only then know the call was there for its effect. `_` says that in the first character, and it says it to the compiler too — the local stops being allocated and stops being something a later edit can accidentally read.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var ignored = queue.TryDequeue(out var unused);
```

Write:

```csharp
_ = queue.TryDequeue(out _);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **This is not `SK0217`.** `arrange-discard-declaration` decides how an *existing* discard is spelled — `var _` against `_` — and never introduces one; this rule introduces one and never restyles one, so the two do not double-count. ⚠ **`_` is a discard only where nothing else claims the name.** A local, a parameter or a field called `_` turns `_ = Foo();` into an assignment to that thing, silently, so every lookup for `_` at the rewrite position must come back empty. ⚠ **Only `out var`, never `out T`.** A discard has no type, so replacing an explicitly typed out-variable can change which overload a call resolves to; `out var` is already typeless in that sense and loses nothing. ⚠ The local's initializer must be a call, a construction, an `await` or a conditional access — something whose *evaluation* is the reason the statement exists. `var x = 5;` is dead code whose repair is deletion, and `_ = 5;` is the same dead code with an assignment bolted on. ⚠ "Never read" is measured as "never mentioned" over the whole member, deliberately: a later assignment is not a read, but dropping a declaration underneath one is a compile error rather than a tidy-up, and a local written twice and read never has no fix here either way. ⚠ `using`, `await using`, `const`, `ref`, attributed and multi-declarator declarations are all left alone. ⚠ **A discard has no type, so whatever the declared type gave the initializer goes with it** ([#402](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/402)). `Local local = new();` became `_ = new();`, which is CS8754; the fix now moves the type into the creation, `_ = new Local();`, when the declared type is a name or a keyword, and declines `T?` (`new T?()` is CS8628 for a reference type) and a tuple type (`new (int, int)()` is CS8181) — an alias to a tuple is a name and compiles. A declaration that runs a user-defined implicit conversion is declined too, because `_ = Make();` compiles and silently stops calling `op_Implicit`. `default`, `[]`, a lambda, a method group, `null`, `stackalloc`, a tuple literal and a conditional all take their type from the declaration as well, and none is an initializer this rule admits. ⚠ **The fix is not safe (#412's audit, measured by running both versions):** The rewrite changes the source text captured by an enclosing `[CallerArgumentExpression]` argument (`Debug.Assert`, `ThrowIfNull`, test asserts).
